candidateRows: Emotivism treats ethical statements as expressions of non-propositional emotion rather than truth-apt reports about a speaker's preferences.
This supplies the con side's central metaethical thesis and directly addresses whether moral claims possess objective truth value.
After the moderator invites his basic view, O'Connor distinguishes emotivism from subjectivism and explains moral language as emotional expression without truth conditions.
Moral predicates label a distinctive emotional response generated alongside factual and psychological descriptions, not an additional moral fact.
The move explains what emotivist moral experience consists in and answers the natural objection that moral language merely reports familiar emotions.
O'Connor separates observable facts and psychological reports from the distinctive imperative-like feeling expressed through terms such as good, bad, right, and wrong.
A materialist moral objectivist must identify what objective oughtness is and explain where it exists or originates if it is not emotion.
The challenge places the explanatory burden at the heart of the debate: identifying the alleged objective moral property and its grounding in reality.
Having stated emotivism, O'Connor contrasts observable material facts with the posited existence of good, bad, should, and ought, then asks what they are and whence they come.
The practical need for evaluative concepts reveals the facts in reality to which those concepts refer; otherwise the terms are arbitrary and dispensable.
This establishes the pro side's governing method for deriving objective moral meaning from the factual conditions that make evaluative language necessary.
O'Connor's demand that objectivists identify what oughtness is and explain its source.
Biddle begins his answer by arguing that needed evaluative terms must have factual referents and introduces the question of which facts generate the need for each concept.
Because only living organisms pursue values to preserve their existence, life is the ultimate factual foundation of value and all evaluative concepts.
The inference from living action to life as the standard of value is the foundational premise of the objectivist morality defended in the debate.
Biddle defines values as objects of action, observes that living beings alone pursue them, and argues that their need to remain alive explains value's factual basis.
For volitional human beings, oughts identify actions required for life, while chosen values and virtues organize the rational pursuit of continued existence and flourishing.
This connects the descriptive fact of living organisms' needs to normative guidance for human agents, addressing the crucial fact-to-ought transition.
O'Connor's challenge that observable facts do not disclose any objective should or ought.
Biddle says ought refers to life-supporting action, invokes human free will and the need for rational guidance, and derives values and virtues from choosing to live.
Moral objectivity is a relation between cognition and life-relevant facts, and using evaluative concepts while severing them from life commits a stolen-concept fallacy.
The move clarifies the defended meaning of objective and gives Biddle's direct response to the claim that moral properties must be free-floating entities.
O'Connor's portrayal of objective oughtness as a mysterious property located in minds, matter, or the space between people.
Biddle rejects the subjective-versus-intrinsic dichotomy, defines objectivity through a mind-fact connection, and argues that life supplies evaluative terms with meaning and necessity.
If immortal volitional people could still care about one another and suffer, ethics would remain applicable despite the complete absence of possible death.
The counterexample directly challenges the claimed necessary dependence of ethics on the life-or-death alternative by separating agency and suffering from mortality.
Biddle's claim that values and ethical guidance ultimately arise from the alternative between continued life and death.
O'Connor imagines an immortality treatment and asks whether conduct toward other conscious beings would cease to matter once nobody could die.
Even if immortal humans retained agency and emotion, ethics would concern maximizing flourishing rather than survival, while real human ethics remains practically grounded in mortality.
The reply both limits the practical relevance of impossible cases and concedes a transformed ethics of flourishing, materially refining the pro position's scope.
O'Connor's immortality scenario offered to show that ethical concern can persist without any prospect of death.
Biddle first emphasizes ethics as practical guidance for mortal life, then grants that immortal but feeling and volitional people would retain an ethics aimed at richer flourishing.
A survival-based egoistic ethic appears unable to condemn recreational animal torture when the act neither threatens the torturer's survival nor frustrates that person's preferences.
The case tests whether the proposed objective standard can explain a strong moral judgment when another being's suffering conflicts with no apparent self-survival interest.
Biddle's derivation of ethical mandates from rational egoism and the requirements of an agent's own life and survival.
O'Connor contrasts social cooperation's benefits with isolated cruelty to an animal and argues that the torturer's survival could remain unaffected or even psychologically enhanced.
Animal abuse is factually immoral because life is the standard of value beyond humans, and gratuitous destruction expresses nihilistic contempt for life.
The move directly applies Biddle's life-based moral standard to a difficult counterexample involving conduct that need not impair the actor's survival.
O'Connor's claim that rational egoism cannot condemn gratuitous animal torture when it benefits the actor.
After O'Connor argues that torturing a dog could benefit its perpetrator, Biddle extends the standard of life to animals and plants and characterizes gratuitous destruction as nihilistic.
Appealing to contempt for life assumes the disputed value of life and therefore argues circularly against someone who does not already share that valuation.
The move attacks the justificatory structure of the life standard by arguing that its answer to the nihilist presupposes precisely what requires establishment.
Biddle's argument that gratuitously harming living things is wrong because doing so treats life as valueless.
Following Biddle's appeal to reverence for life, O'Connor asks how that appeal can persuade a person who denies life's value and says the offered answer restates its premise.
Life is not intrinsically valuable; rather, a person's choice to remain alive logically precedes evaluation and creates the need for values and action.
This is a direct account of the proposed factual foundation for value, distinguishing the view from intrinsic-value theories and locating value in chosen life.
O'Connor's circularity objection and his assumption that Biddle treats life as intrinsically valuable.
Biddle narrows the standard primarily to choosing human agents, denies that his own life has intrinsic value, and argues that choosing continued existence logically precedes all evaluation.
A pre-moral choice to live cannot supply objective normativity, because any foundational claim that one should remain alive is either objective or leaves the moral edifice nonobjective.
The move challenges the transition from a chosen end to objective moral requirements, targeting the central grounding claim rather than a peripheral implication.
Biddle's claim that the choice to remain alive is pre-moral, pre-rational, and foundational for every subsequent value.
After discussing suicide and action, O'Connor asks whether staying alive is objectively right and argues that a nonobjective foundational choice cannot generate an objective moral system.
The requirements of human life generate universal moral principles, including individual rights, because each person's life belongs to that person and requires action on personal judgment.
The move supplies the key bridge from life as a standard to interpersonal morality and political rights, addressing how egoism can prohibit enslaving another person.
O'Connor's contention that a possibly nonobjective choice to live cannot support objective prohibitions such as the ban on murder.
Biddle rejects the premise that one objectively should remain alive, then uses slavery to argue that human nature and ownership of one's life yield general moral principles and rights.
A murderer who values his own life and genuinely benefits from killing an innocent person is a counterexample to grounding moral obligation in the actor's life and flourishing.
The hypothetical tests whether rational egoism condemns an advantageous killing without importing the victim's value or the actor's empathy into the foundation.
Biddle's claim that human life is valuable only when chosen and pursued consistently with respecting other people's rights.
O'Connor distinguishes the moral actor's survival from the victim's and asks about an unempathetic murderer whose own life and flourishing would improve through an innocent death.
Rational egoism does not license whatever appears advantageous, because rational agents must respect rights and may confine violent psychopaths regardless of those psychopaths' values.
The move answers the advantageous-murder objection by denying an unconstrained conception of egoism and connecting life, rights, moral principles, and coercive protection.
O'Connor's hypothetical in which an unempathetic psychopath materially benefits from murdering an innocent rights-respecting person.
Biddle argues that egoism considers the full context of human life, rejects rights violations for apparent gain, and says dangerous violent people may be confined under life-based principles.
Invoking rights to constrain rational egoism presupposes the objective moral properties under dispute and does not explain why an egoist should care about another person's rights.
The objection targets a potential circularity in the proposed derivation of interpersonal obligation, asking whether rights are independently grounded or merely assumed.
Biddle's reliance on individual rights to explain why egoism forbids beneficial violence and permits confinement of dangerous people.
After Biddle appeals repeatedly to rights, O'Connor argues that this relies on the objective morality being justified and asks what rights are within a survival-centered egoistic framework.

A psychopath who can choose between life-promoting and life-ending actions remains capable of the choice said to generate ethics, so excluding that person from morality undermines the life-death grounding.
The move identifies an apparent inconsistency between the proposed sufficient basis for moral agency and Biddle's later exclusion of a cognitively capable psychopath.
Biddle's claim that a sufficiently broken psychopath is outside morality and lacks any capacity to be moral or immoral.
When Biddle places the psychopath outside morality, O'Connor notes that the person can still make choices affecting continued life, which had earlier been presented as ethics' basis.
Moral concepts concern the normal characteristics of human beings, so a psychopath lacking the capacity to recognize others' ownership of their lives is an exceptional, incomplete case.
The move defends the life-based account against an abnormal-case counterexample by explaining how general concepts and principles accommodate impaired members of a class.
O'Connor's argument that a life-directed psychopath contradicts the claimed intrinsic connection between life-or-death choice and moral agency.
Biddle explains that concepts refer to normal class characteristics, compares the psychopath to an incomplete or injured instance, and grounds confinement in danger to other people's lives.
Individual rights recognize the factual human need for freedom to act on rational judgment, while those who violate others' rights may forfeit their own freedom.
The move connects factual requirements of human life to moral and political rights, directly illustrating how the pro side derives normative principles from life.
O'Connor's psychopath example and challenge to the asserted right to confine someone who threatens others.
After O'Connor questions the standard behind an asserted right to imprison a psychopath, Biddle defines rights through freedom, rational agency, and protection from force.
Calling one kind of brain broken cannot be objectively justified without a nonmajoritarian standard beyond each person's subjective view of how a brain should function.
The move attacks the alleged objectivity of Biddle's standard by arguing that competing psychological constitutions cannot be ranked without importing subjective norms.
Biddle's claim that the psychopath has a broken mind and may lose freedom because he threatens the rights of others.
At the close of the main exchange, O'Connor imagines a psychopath and non-psychopath disputing which brain is broken after everyone else has died.
Emotions register a person's values but are not instruments of knowledge; rational inquiry identifies life as the objective standard of moral value.
This directly distinguishes Objectivist moral cognition from emotivism and states the pro side's central route from rational investigation to objective value.
The audience proposal that emotivism might coexist with or develop into Objectivism through aggregated emotional approval.
An audience member asks whether widespread emotional approval could ground objective goodness; Biddle answers that emotions experience values but do not discover moral truth.
Emotivism explains moral phenomena such as differential concern for animals and the widespread incest taboo more naturally than rational egoism does.
The move supplies explanatory support for the con position by arguing that emotional reactions account for persistent moral judgments that resist rational derivation.
Biddle's claim that emotion merely experiences independently rational values and cannot determine moral right and wrong.
Following Biddle's rejection of emotivism, O'Connor argues that resemblance-based concern for animals and aversion to incest fit an emotional account of morality.
The choice to live is pre-rational only in the technical sense that reasons and all other values matter conditionally upon choosing life.
The move clarifies the foundational conditional structure of the pro theory, explaining why rational justification operates only after life has been selected as an end.
Asked to clarify an earlier statement, Biddle distinguishes an adult's reason-involving deliberation about suicide from the technical dependence of reasons and values on choosing life.
Emotivism can concede that its ethical advocacy lacks objective binding force while maintaining that rational conclusions can bind in an amoral sense.
The move answers a major self-defeat objection by separating rational entailment from moral obligation and accepting emotive rather than objective ethical persuasion.
The audience objection that rationally arguing for emotivism presupposes objective rational and moral obligations that undermine emotivism.
O'Connor accepts that his moral advocacy is emotive, distinguishes personal values from objective duties, and argues that rational inference need not itself be moral.
Human life as the standard of value means flourishing through full human capacities, not mere biological survival, and is more fundamental than happiness.
This clarifies the core pro standard against equivocation, integrating biological existence, consciousness, happiness, virtue, and freedom within flourishing human life.
The challenge that guaranteed physical survival and psychopath psychology show that survival cannot be the objective moral standard.
Responding to an audience question about physical and psychological survival, Biddle says life means survival as a fully functioning human being and therefore flourishing.
Universal human rights do not literally exist under materialism; treating them as useful fictions can nevertheless improve human life and conduct.
The answer applies the con side's antirealist framework to rights, separating practical endorsement from truth and reinforcing the denial of objective moral entities.
Asked whether materialism can justify universal human rights, O'Connor denies their literal existence but compares acting as if they exist to a useful safety convention.
Evidence for objective morality depends on a definition of moral goodness, and rational egoism fails because human life or flourishing does not adequately capture ordinary ethical meaning.
The move states the con side's burden for moral realism and locates its central objection to Biddle in semantic adequacy rather than merely denying that life exists.
Biddle's objective ethical theory identifying human life or flourishing as the factual standard and content of moral value.
O'Connor explains that different realist theories require different proofs, then argues that life-based definitions omit familiar ethical concern for others and animals.
Goodness and value are kinds of fact concerning what promotes human life, while morality is the code of values guiding the life-shaping choices and actions of an individual.
The move gives the pro theory's defining bridge from descriptive life-supporting facts to evaluative concepts and then to a practical code of morality.
O'Connor's contention that life and flourishing do not define goodness in a way that captures what people mean by ethics.
Immediately after O'Connor requests a definition that captures ethical meaning, Biddle defines good, value, and morality by reference to facts about sustaining human life.
Animals lack the conceptual and rational capacities that distinguish human beings as rights-bearing moral agents.
This rational-capacity distinction supplies the principal basis for Craig's different moral treatment of human beings and nonhuman animals.
The audience challenge that prioritizing life makes permissible animal killing inconsistent with condemning animal torture.
Craig answers the animal-treatment objection by separating instinct-driven animals from conceptual human agents capable of understanding and respecting rights.
General biological values must be distinguished from moral values, which arise only within the sphere of human choice.
The distinction explains why valuing animal life or condemning needless suffering does not entail granting animals human moral rights.
The follow-up claim that condemning attacks on living things appears to be a moral value judgment inconsistent with killing animals.
Craig distinguishes life-serving values generally from chosen human moral values, denies animals human rights, and proposes an intermediate form of respect for some animals.
Painlessly killing an animal is categorically different from killing a person because an animal cannot conceptualize or project its future.
This claim directly supports the disputed permissibility of humane animal slaughter while preserving the theory's stronger protection for human life.
Alex's objection that accepting animal killing while rejecting animal torture appears to value suffering more highly than life.
Craig argues that humane slaughter must minimize pain and that animals occupy a different category because they cannot conceive of a future life.
Eating animals can remain permissible for nutrition and enjoyment because animals lack rights, provided their deaths involve no unnecessary pain.
The move states Craig's operative justification for meat consumption and identifies unnecessary pain, rather than animal killing itself, as the limiting condition.
The audience challenge asking whether killing animals merely for taste remains justified when their nutritional value can be obtained otherwise.
Craig packages taste and nutrition together, says animal death for food does not greatly trouble him, and grounds the conclusion in a sharp rights distinction.
Humane animal husbandry and slaughter serve life-supporting purposes, unlike destroying a living thing solely from contempt for life.
The purposive-motive distinction is Craig's direct resolution of the alleged inconsistency between condemning flower destruction and permitting meat consumption.
Alex's challenge that killing an animal for taste seems inconsistent with calling the destruction of a flower for enjoyment nihilistic.
Craig contrasts contemptuous destruction with caring for animals and killing them painlessly for nutrition and joy, which he characterizes as non-nihilistic purposes.
A suicidal person's life may not be taken without consent, although consensual assistance in suicide can be morally permissible.
The distinction applies Craig's rights framework to consent, showing that another person's present wish to die does not independently authorize homicide.
The audience hypothetical asking whether killing someone who already intends to commit suicide would nevertheless count as immoral murder.
Craig says unauthorized killing remains murder because only the person controls that choice, while a voluntary contract for assisted suicide can be legitimate.
The intuitive obviousness of a moral judgment does not establish objective truth because contrary evaluations can seem equally obvious to different agents.
This directly contests the inference from shared moral intuition to objective morality and articulates the central epistemic defense of Alex's emotivist position.
The questioner's claim that the non-arbitrary difference between a flourishing person and a destructive person is plainly evident.
Alex grants that the contrast feels obvious to him while arguing that an opposed response may feel equally obvious to a psychopath, so intuition is insufficient.
Calling a sacrificial killing moral expresses an emotive endorsement rather than reporting an objective moral property.
The answer applies emotivism to a concrete life-and-death case and clarifies how Alex can use ordinary moral vocabulary without asserting moral truth values.
The audience question asking whether it can ever be moral to kill an unwilling human or nonhuman animal.
Alex endorses killing one cow to save many people but explains that describing the act as right reports his emotional stance and likely shared feelings.
Moral emotions accompany judgments of good and bad, but the judgment itself expresses a life-based evaluation rather than an emotion.
This is a concise final statement of the core disagreement: emotions are consequences of cognition for Craig, not the semantic content of moral claims.
Alex's account that assertions of moral rightness translate into expressions of the speaker's feelings about the situation.
Craig acknowledges that moral evaluation is emotionally charged while maintaining that moral language identifies something as supportive or destructive of life.
